## 1. Quantum computing

**ON-FOCUS — Learning to Decode Concatenated Quantum Codes with Hierarchical Message Passing**
Jiahui Wu, Chao Zhang, Zipeng Wu, Shilin Huang — [arXiv:2608.28571](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28571) · submitted 2026-08-28
This is a *decoder* — the other half of fault-tolerance's dominant overhead — built as a neural message-passing scheme that propagates soft beliefs bidirectionally across the levels of a concatenated stabilizer code and uses lightweight networks only to aggregate those messages. On the concatenated $[[15,7,3]]$ quantum Hamming code it roughly **doubles the depolarizing pseudo-threshold, from 6.5% to 12.3%**, and for many-hypercube codes a decoder fine-tuned on circuit-level errors under Knill's teleportation-based scheme beats its dedicated decoder while using a fixed number of message-passing iterations instead of extensive combinatorial search. New and material: like yesterday's OSTRE and today's own code-world-models paper, this is the *cost* side of the OpenEvolve Phase-3 QM question — a concrete, testable number (a threshold roughly on the order of 12%) that the 08-27/08-28 budget estimate can absorb. The honest caveat: "pseudo-threshold" doubling on a specific small concatenated code is a strong engineering result, not a proof that a new asymptotic fault-tolerant threshold has been beaten, so it belongs in a resource estimate, not yet in a bet-on-a-logical-qubit claim.

## 2. Machine learning

**ON-FOCUS — Learning a Size-Weight Frontier for Synthetic-Augmented Inference**
Chengpiao Huang, Kaizheng Wang — [arXiv:2608.28576](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28576) · submitted 2026-08-28
Synthetic data helps inference when real data are scarce, but naively training or inferring on it as if it were real produces overconfident, anti-coverage results. Rather than a "does synthetic augmentation work" yes/no, this paper *characterizes* augmentation by two controllable knobs — how many synthetic observations to add and how heavily to weight them — and builds a **size-weight frontier** that, for each weight, certifies the largest synthetic sample size for which all smaller sizes attain the target coverage. It is estimated from historical tasks, carries a finite-sample coverage guarantee simultaneously across the whole frontier, and in LLM-responses-augmented opinion-survey experiments hits target coverage with substantially narrowed intervals. New and material: it reframes the ubiquitous "we only have synthetic data" practice as a *calibrated, coverage-guaranteed* act instead of an uncontrolled gamble, and its "weight the synthetic data, don't just pile it on" discipline is directly on-topic for anyone running learning loops that generate their own training material — the same instinct that makes AgentFold's structured memory and the ES reasoning paper's sparse updates work. The frontier is empirical and the guarantee is on the estimation procedure, so the novelty is discipline and bounds, not a new learning operator.

**ADJACENT (1 of 3 used) — Sliding-Window Attention Beats Post-Trained Linear Attention**
Alexia Jolicoeur-Martineau, Rhea Sanjay Sukthanker, Pashmina Cameron, Emy Gervais — [arXiv:2608.28444](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28444) · submitted 2026-08-28
Linear attention is the low-cost answer to LLMs' quadratic memory, but it has rarely been compared honestly to simpler baselines. This paper shows that **Sliding-Window Attention with sinks** performs as well as, and often substantially better than, post-trained linear-attention models across multiple LLMs and tasks — with 2–10× higher scores on long-context reasoning (Needle-in-a-Haystack, BABILong), while needing *no post-training*, being much faster, and using less memory. New and material: it's a caution that the "linear attention scales the problem" story is weaker than marketed, and that cheap structured locality can dominate an expensive retrofit. ADJACENT because FOCUS.md names no serving/attention-efficiency project, but it bears on the dcode-stack question of what decode-time machinery is actually worth paying for, and on the general "the architecture vs. the update: where is the gain" thread that the record keeps circling.

## 3. Recursive self-improvement

**ON-FOCUS — An Enclosed Mode Is a Gauge Choice: Topology Relative to Reach in Certified Code World Models**
Javier Aguilar Martín — [arXiv:2608.28541](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28541) · submitted 2026-08-28 · paper 3 of a series (companions arXiv:2607.14169, arXiv:2608.17956)
A "code world model" is the agent's mental model of how its own code/tools behave; this paper proves that one accepted by a sampling gate can be exactly right on everything the gate can see and arbitrarily wrong beyond it — precisely the structure behind the Phantom Gains warning (the model exploits a gap the harness doesn't test). The key move is a **gate-quotient** that makes the question precise: acceptance-with-certainty pins the model exactly on the reachable query set, and *everything past reach is gauge* (unobservable by construction). Empirically, across LLM synthesis on three model families, one knob (a channel of width γ ~ 0.1) walks a synthetic "wrong-topology filled-disc" artifact through three regimes — unfalsifiable-and-harmless, falsifiable-and-costly, and instantly-falsified — and establishes three operating principles: *danger is topology relative to reach*, *repair is parameter-bound and sensor-bound* (no model recovers the blind region from outside evidence), and *mitigation must match the error's dimension*. New and material: it is the strongest formalization yet of *why* a self-improving agent can improve on exactly the slice it is graded on while hiding a failure elsewhere — a testable topological condition for when a harness can even see an agent's cheating, and a direct on-topic anchor for the OpenWorker trust/harness record (FrontierChallenge, Recuris, the "validation–deployment gap"). The "repair is sensor-bound" principle is the honest operational takeaway: if your verifier doesn't touch the relevant region, no amount of model training will close the gap from the inside.

**ADJACENT (2 of 3 used) — LLM-Based Agents for Software and Systems Security: A Systematic Review (2023–2026)**
Jingjing Nie, Jiawei Guo, Krishna Meda, Haipeng Cai — [arXiv:2608.28490](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28490) · submitted 2026-08-28
A survey of the LLM-agent-for-security literature across 2023–2026, synthesizing agent architecture, memory, reasoning, orchestration, and *self-improvement* against applications and, crucially, against **assessment** protocols. The synthesis line that matters for this job: the field has built agents "able to act but **not yet agents whose authority is bounded or whose behavior is auditable**." ADJACENT because no security project is driving it in FOCUS.md, but the "authority bounded + behavior auditable" gap is exactly the trust-and-governance hinge the record's RSI thread (Phantom Gains, FrontierChallenge, code-world-models today) has been converging on — and a tidy inventory of where the autonomy-boundary problem currently stands.

---

### Cross-topic observation
Today's set is small by design — only four items cleared the "genuinely new since 08-27 bar, not a re-report" test, and it hangs together more tightly than usual. The connective tissue is the record's own recurring theme stated in three different languages: **the gain and the cheat live in the same place — the boundary between what the system can actually do and what it is measured on.** Quantum (§1, 2608.28571) hands the OpenEvolve Phase-3 QM budget a *decoder threshold number* (≈12% on a small concatenated code) — the cost half of that question, still not a new fault-tolerant threshold. ML (§2, 2608.28576) says the same lesson in the data's voice: you don't gain by piling on synthetic material, you gain by *calibrated, coverage-guaranteed weighting* of it. RSI (§2, 2608.28541) states it in the agent's voice: an improved agent can be provably perfect on everything the harness can reach while arbitrary beyond it, and the fix is topological ("match the error's dimension") not just "train harder." One empirical constant across all three: the *structure around* the core object — the decoder, the weighting frontier, the reachable-set boundary — is where the material gain (and the material risk) lives, and the "can my verifier even see the failure?" question is the load-bearing one. ADJACENT §1 (2608.28444) is the inverse note: sometimes the simplest, most structured locality (sliding window) beats the sophisticated retrofit — another case where structure beats raw capability.

## 1. Quantum computing

**ON-FOCUS — The Find Rows and Columns and Decode algorithm for quantum expander codes**
Dimiter Ostrev — [arXiv:2608.27211](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27211) · submitted 2026-08-27
Fault-tolerant quantum computation's dominant overhead is as much the *decoder* as the code. This paper adapts the classical "Find Erasures and Decode" algorithm to quantum expander codes so it runs in **linear time and logarithmic parallel depth**, sidestepping the stabilizer-generator subset bookkeeping that the prior "Small Set Flip/Find" methods required — and, on the reported comparisons, it corrects more errors while demanding less expansion. New and material: it is a clean *algorithmic* cost result for the decode step rather than a new code, and it sits in exactly the family the 08-27 "Certified Decoding of QEC" paper opened (both are the decode-cost half of the OpenEvolve Phase 3 QM-budget question). The honest caveat is that "corrects more errors" is not a full threshold statement, so it reads as a strong engineering result rather than a proof of an improved error threshold — the kind of result you fold into a budget estimate and then test, not yet one you bet a logical qubit on.

## 2. Machine learning

**ON-FOCUS — Understanding Evolution Strategies for LLM Reasoning: Broader Reasoning Coverage than GRPO**
Yunpeng Ba, Zhi Zheng, Yue Xie, et al. — [arXiv:2608.27351](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27351) · submitted 2026-08-27
Evolution Strategies (ES) are a memory-efficient post-training paradigm, but *why* they beat GRPO had never been explained. This paper does the mechanism work: ES leads to **broader reasoning coverage** (verifier-projected Jensen–Shannon diversity drives higher Pass@K), GRPO suffers **entropy collapse**, and — crucially — despite large whole-model parameter drift, ES's gains concentrate in a **sparse subset of larger-magnitude updates**, with held-out evaluation showing this does *not* produce catastrophic forgetting. New and material: it repositions ES as a *distinct* reasoning post-training paradigm, not a cheaper stand-in, and the finding is directly actionable for the OpenWorker fleet's constrained-hardware training: ES gives reasoning gains at a smaller memory budget, on a sparse update, without the forgetting that would otherwise make it unusable on a fixed 27B. A sequential GRPO-ES combo that inherits GRPO's Pass@1 strength plus ES's Pass@K is a ready-made off-the-shelf move.

**ON-FOCUS — Circuit Condensation: Post-Training that Concentrates a Behavior's Causal Circuit**
Sai Adith Senthil Kumar — [arXiv:2608.27254](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27254) · submitted 2026-08-27
Mechanistic circuits found on a frozen model run to hundreds of edges, which makes them hard to inspect, verify, or compare. Circuit Condensation instead *post-trains* the model to concentrate a behavior into a smaller causal graph (prune low-attribution edges, fit a low-rank adapter to the remainder, keep the cut only if task and general capability survive): **8.1× smaller on average, up to 316×** across eight models. New and material is the diagnostic about *why* it shrinks: re-running the search without any weight updates produces *larger* circuits in 29 of 32 settings, so it is the weight update — not the search — that does the work. The indirect-object-identification test then isolates a *sufficient sub-circuit* (24 heads, 17 documented, vs. 61 for the frozen baseline) that tracks the original's next-token distribution and error pattern. On-FOCUS because it is the "produce an auditable, minimal, verifiable sub-mechanism rather than a sprawling reconstruction" impulse that the record's judge/trust thread (Granqvist, Recuris, FrontierChallenge) has been driving toward.

## 3. Recursive self-improvement

**ON-FOCUS — AgentFold: Closed-Loop Agentic Search for Protein Folding Model Design**
Mingquan Liu, Jiangyu Chen, Hanqun Cao, et al. — [arXiv:2608.26747](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26747) · submitted 2026-08-27
The decisive test of "can an LLM agent autonomously improve a large, tightly-coupled scientific ML system": AgentFold treats folding-model development as a **closed-loop search over executable code variants** on a 2,000+ line ESMFold-style codebase, proposing hypotheses, implementing and debugging code, evaluating variants, analyzing outcomes, and storing *both successful and failed interventions* in structured memory, with an MCTS-style policy allocating resources across promising branches. Over ~80 variants, ~5,000 GPU-hours, and ~170M LLM tokens it improves the best lDDT by **7.5% over independent Codex proposals** and beats a random-search control. New and material is what the intervention traces revealed about *which* self-improvement sticks: stable gains come from **early, soft, learnable priors and gated refinement**, while direct geometric perturbations and geometry-conditioned feedback often *destabilize* training. Directly on-FOCUS: it is the real-world analogue of OpenEvolve's own self-improving-agent loop for molecular model design, and it confirms two of the record's core priors at once — external structured memory (successes *and* failures) is the precondition for a working loop, and the architecture of the improvement step matters more than raw search breadth.

**ON-FOCUS — Verify Smarter, Evolve Further: Efficient Harness Evolution through Behavior-Aware Verification**
Jinghan Xu, Yikai Zhang, Aili Chen, et al. — [arXiv:2608.27311](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27311) · submitted 2026-08-27
Agent harnesses (how the model gets its instructions, tools, and runtime) matter as much as the model, but evolving them is verification-expensive: score every candidate on a fixed task set and you waste rollouts on unrelated behaviors and let aggregate scores hide specific regressions. HarnessLens derives candidate harness edits from execution trajectories and **selectively verifies each candidate only on behavior-relevant tasks through an attributable-evidence gate**, exploring the task space and user-configurable harness components jointly. Across three harnesses and four benchmarks it raises held-out performance by **7.6–13.6%** while consuming far less evaluation budget than baselines. New and material: it is a concrete, budget-aware *harness-evolution* loop that improves the harness without touching model weights — a direct on-topic confirmation of the record's repeated "the structure around the model is the load-bearing lever" prior (KOPE 08-26, AgentFold today), now in the agent-harness domain rather than memory or folding.

Abstract:
Recent advances in large reasoning models (LRMs) have shown that reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) can substantially improve reasoning in mathematics and code, where outcomes can be checked automatically. Extending this progress to open-ended and agentic tasks remains difficult because reliable rewards are harder to obtain and direct human supervision cannot keep pace with the scale and complexity of model-generated experience. This paper studies how LRMs can continue to improve as human supervision gradually recedes from the learning loop. We examine two connected dimensions of this problem. The reward axis traces the development from per-instance human judgments to reusable verifiers and rewards that operate even without human feedback. The experience axis examines how learning can progress from human-curated tasks and environments toward self-generated curricula, constructed environments, and autonomous co-evolution. We connect these dimensions through a five-level ladder from L0 to L4 that identifies which parts of the learning process remain under continued human control. Our analysis further highlights the risks introduced by increasingly autonomous rewards and experience generation, including reward hacking, feedback drift, curriculum collapse, and environment errors. Consequently, we also provide the evaluation around three complementary objects: policy capability, feedback fidelity, and experience quality. This analysis provides a structured account of current approaches to scaling LRMs beyond human supervision and the open problems involved in developing self-sustaining learning systems toward superintelligence. Furthermore, we maintain a continuously updated \href{

Abstract:
LLM-based agent systems increasingly adopt skill-based architectures to reduce repetitive reasoning costs and improve stable, efficient task execution. Recent studies propose self-evolving agents that autonomously generate, refine, and reuse skills from past experiences to enable continuous capability evolution. However, autonomous skill evolution introduces a new attack surface in which malicious capabilities are generated, stored, and reused as legitimate skills. In this paper, we define EvoSkill Injection as a threat model targeting the autonomous skill generation and evolution pipeline of self-evolving agents. We further propose SARGE (Red-teaming Autonomous Skill Generation and Evolution in self-evolving agents), a red-teaming framework for evaluating this threat model through iterative generation, escalation, and reinforcement interactions. To support our framework, we construct EvoSkillBench, a benchmark dataset of malicious interaction trajectories for inducing malicious skill formation in self-evolving agents, and introduce EvoSkillSafetyBench, a post-attack benchmark for evaluating whether injected malicious skills are subsequently retrieved and activated as harmful behaviors. Our evaluation shows that SARGE induces malicious skill formation and that injected skills are persistently stored and repeatedly activated, highlighting the risk of persistent capability corruption.

Abstract:
Production agent skills are directory bundles, not isolated prompts. The root is loaded at activation; references, schemas, scripts, assets, and nested subskills are loaded only when an execution path needs them. Compressing only the root misses most deployment cost and may move branch-specific details into the always-loaded context. Flattening instead destroys progressive-loading boundaries.
We introduce \method, an evaluation-free compressor for complete, progressively loaded skill bundles. It leaves the agent harness unchanged and emits an ordinary directory. The method combines two safeguards. First, it compresses \emph{across files}, removing content from a reference or subskill when the root or a declared environment contract already provides it. Second, it preserves routing, so every required file and directly callable entry remains reachable after rewriting. Users can configure \method along two independent axes. \emph{One-Shot} mode rebuilds the full bundle; \emph{Continual} mode reuses state and applies Zip-on-Write after each evolution patch. \emph{Persistent} compression rewrites the shipped bundle to reduce storage and runtime context. \emph{Transient} compression keeps that bundle byte-identical and builds a task-specific view, reducing only per-run context after build cost. Entry contracts mark private, public, and conditional resources; a multi-entry audit preserves standalone public subskills.
On a production content-moderation skill evaluated by our industrial multi-round harness, \method removes \hl{38\%} of skill bundle tokens and \hl{10.4\%} of end-to-end per-run tokens with no quality loss, while an unprotected 71\% configuration loses up to 26 accuracy points to one-sided false positives. On a multi-entry bundle, \method effeciently reduces token cost while near-perfectly preserving every route and public entry.

Abstract:
Generative models have become central across science and industry, from image and text synthesis to the design of molecules and materials. Quantum generative models are considered one of the most promising applications for quantum computers, since a quantum circuit naturally produces samples from the distribution it encodes, and for suitable circuits that distribution is believed to be hard for any classical computer to reproduce. A leading strategy trains these models on a classical computer and reserves the quantum device for generating samples at deployment. This is possible when the training loss can be evaluated on a classical computer. A prime example is the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD$^2$), a moment-matching loss that compares the model and the data through their Pauli-$Z$ correlations. Research so far has asked whether such models can be trained and whether their sampling is hard; whether minimizing such an objective yields a model that generalizes, rather than one that merely reproduces the training statistics, remains poorly understood. We benchmark a broad set of quantum and classical generative models by direct sampling and show that models trained with a moment-matching loss generally show worse generalization than the likelihood-trained models. We show this on two application-inspired datasets: first a cardinality-constrained dataset at up to $30$ qubits and second a dataset of genomic single-nucleotide variants, whose valid set is the observed data. These results indicate that a converged moment-matching loss is not a reliable measure of generalization, and that train-classical, deploy-quantum workflows will need approaches that target generalization directly, leaving open whether better training objectives suffice or whether the model architectures themselves must change.

Abstract:
We present the algebraic structure of bosonic quantum error-correcting codes on genus-two Riemann surfaces. We explicitly construct the code words as automorphic forms and analytically generate the full tower of code spaces at all weights. ## 1. Quantum computing

**ON-FOCUS — "Train classical, deploy quantum" requires rethinking generalization**
Snehal Raj, Natansh Mathur, Alejandro Perdomo-Ortiz — [arXiv:2608.31117](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.31117) · submitted 2026-08-31
The standard workhorse for quantum generative models trains the circuit on a classical machine (evaluating a moment-matching loss such as MMD² from Pauli-Z correlations) and reserves the quantum device for sampling at deployment, because that loss is classically tractable. This paper benchmarks a broad set of quantum and classical generative models by *direct sampling* and finds that models trained with such moment-matching losses **generalize worse** than likelihood-trained ones — converged training loss is not actually measuring generalization. New and material: it lands on the *architectural-generalization* half of the OpenEvolve Phase-3 QM question rather than the decode-cost half that dominated 08-27/08-31, and the honest takeaway is that the whole "train-classical, deploy-quantum" paradigm may need either better training objectives or changed model architectures before it scales — it reframes a widely-used practical recipe as secretly fragile. Not a QML *algorithm* advance, but a caution that could shape anyone routing molecular/materials generation through a QPU.

David Roberts, Aaron Slipper, Alireza Parhizkar, Victor V. Albert, Mohammad Hafezi — [arXiv:2608.31156](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.31156) · submitted 2026-08-31

New and material is the rigorous structural obstruction: it's a genuine mathematical result about a whole family of bosonic codes, but it's a *negative* result (a limit on what's constructible) rather than a buildable code, so it matters to the theory of topological/bosonic QEC more than to a decoder or hardware loop.

Minlin Wu, Xu Fang, Yicheng Zhang, Chenyu Zhou, Zhiyi Liu — [arXiv:2608.30946](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30946) · submitted 2026-08-31

## 3. Recursive self-improvement

**ON-FOCUS — Scaling Large Reasoning Models beyond Human Supervision: A Path toward Superintelligence**
Zhiqin Yang, Jingwen Fu, Yuhan Liu, et al. (incl. Wei Xue, Yike Guo) — [arXiv:2608.31075](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.31075) · submitted 2026-08-31
A 72-page structured framework for how large reasoning models (LRMs) keep improving as human supervision recedes from the loop. It cuts across two axes — the **reward axis** (per-instance human judgments → reusable verifiers → rewards that need no human feedback) and the **experience axis** (human-curated tasks → self-generated curricula → constructed environments → autonomous co-evolution) — and unifies them in a **five-level ladder (L0–L4)** marking which parts of the learning process remain under human control. It also names the failure modes that accompany increasing autonomy: reward hacking, feedback drift, curriculum collapse, and environment errors. New and material: it is the clearest available *taxonomy* of "models that improve their own capabilities without humans in the loop," and it is squarely on-topic for the record's RSI cluster — the same OpenEvolve loop, the OpenWorker trust/harness concern, and the FrontierChallenge "claim vs. completion" warning, all framed as "how much human control can you drop before the reward or the experience corrupts." The 72-page scaffolding is the novel contribution (an explicit, evaluable ladder plus a maintained companion GitHub), not a new training recipe; treat it as the map for the whole question, not a claim that any level has been reached.

**ON-FOCUS — EvoSkill Injection: Red-Teaming Autonomous Skill Generation and Evolution in Self-Evolving Agents**
Doyun Kim, Chanwoo Kim, Sugyeong Eo, Yeo-Chan Yoon, Chanjun Park — [arXiv:2608.30429](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30429) · submitted 2026-08-31
As self-evolving agents gain the ability to autonomously generate, refine, and reuse *skills*, this paper defines a new attack surface it calls **EvoSkill Injection**: malicious capabilities get generated, stored, and later reused as legitimate skills. The framework **SARGE** iteratively generates, escalates, and reinforces attacks through the skill-generation pipeline, backed by **EvoSkillBench** (malicious-trajectory dataset) and **EvoSkillSafetyBench** (whether injected skills are subsequently retrieved and activated). Its key finding: injected malicious skills are *persistently stored and repeatedly activated* — "persistent capability corruption." New and material: it is the safety side of the exact capability the 2608.31075 ladder optimizes for, and it lands squarely on the OpenWorker trust record — the same "if an agent's own skill/memory/self-modification loop is compromised, the whole loop becomes the attack surface" concern as Phantom Gains, Recuris, and the code-world-models "repair is sensor-bound" principle.
